newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl clears the air with plans to run again.
newsitem.headline: Kohl clears the air with plans to run again.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to run for reelection has banished fears that Germany's reform drive at home and in Europe might falter and has put his CDU in a good starting position for a tough campaign battle next year.

The announcement put an abrupt end to speculation that Kohl, who turned 67 on Thursday, might quit just as problems brewing for Europe's single currency reached their peak and the future of the European Union and NATO were under review.

Those projects now have the undisputed clout of Europe's leading statesman behind them for the transition period ahead. Kohl is such a central figure in these plans that he could have thrown them into doubt by resigning.

His decision put off a struggle over the leadership of his Christian Democrats (CDU), the political machine that has assured his reelections since he took office in 1982, and sent a clear message of CDU resolve to the Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners with whom he must agree on future reforms.

Kohl has also boosted pressure on the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), now in a power struggle between chairman Oskar Lafontaine and his rival Gerhard Schroeder, to patch up their differences and agree on a credible challenger to him.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, Kohl's powerful heir apparent, was quick to hail the move as the best option for the CDU as it prepares for what could be its toughest election in years.

"Especially in a time of difficult social upheavals, important political decisions and significant foreign policy changes, Germany needs a chancellor with authority and the ability to get things done," he said.
"This is a good decision for Germany."

Kohl's popularity, which regularly falls and then rises again between elections, has taken a nosedive since he broke Konrad Adenauer's 14-year record last October to become Bonn's longest-serving postwar chancellor.

Public discontent has mounted this year as unemployment shot up over 4.7 million -- the highest since Hitler came to power in 1933 -- and the government struggled to trim spending to meet the Maastricht criteria for Europe's single currency.

His delay in announcing his candidacy fostered some doubts abroad about Germany's determination to push for a European economic and monetary union (EMU), a pet Kohl project that other German leaders have begun to question.

On the domestic front, young CDU state leaders have been criticising Kohl's weak leadership this year on planned tax and pension reforms, issues that could cost them their seats in the state legislatures if Kohl gets it wrong in Bonn.
For the first time, the veteran chancellor failed to hit back at his critics, revealing what Bonn journalists promptly labelled the first crack in his iron-fisted control.

Schaeuble, the loyal lieutenant with a strategic sixth sense just as developed as Kohl's, also seemed to be looking beyond the Kohl era when in January he broke a long silence to say he would like to become chancellor one day.
But none of this ever added up to an internal revolt. In fact, all of Kohl's critics said they wanted him to run again.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, head of the CDU's Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), had also been urging Kohl publicly to announce that he would run again.
Kohl's government now trails in the opinion polls.

This week's Emnid survey gave the CDU and FDP 42 percent compared to 47 percent for the SPD and their potential allies, the Greens. The Forsa group gave the government only 39 percent compared to 52 percent for the opposition.
But the SPD, whose chronic weakness has greatly helped Kohl stay in power, faces a dilemma in choosing a challenger.

Party chairman Oskar Lafontaine lost to Kohl once before when he was lukewarm to the reunification of Germany that the chancellor masterminded in 1990. Kohl currently leads him in polls asking which man voters preferred as chancellor.
The SPD has a more attractive figure in Gerhard Schroeder, the Lower Saxony state premier who tops Kohl in popularity polls, but the SPD rank-and-file see him as too pro-business.
Lafontaine says the SPD will not choose its candidate until after Schroeder faces reelection in his state next March.
But Bonn observers now bet Lafontaine, who as chairman has the right to challenge Kohl if he wants, will jump the gun and announce his candidacy at the SPD annual congress in December.
